extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of virtue ethics / readers of Aristotle
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative criteria for moral virtues (especially Courage, Self-Mastery, and Liberality) as presented in Books III–IV of the Nicomachean Ethics. Focus is on how to recognize the mean, excess, and defect for these virtues and their motivating features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — not from compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is not truly Brave if their action is due to compulsion; true courage is not the result of being forced into danger but arises from a sense of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: commanders who compel troops (Hector's method) or place obstacles behind soldiers produce apparent bravery by compulsion, not genuine courage. Compulsion is contrasted with honour-motivated action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — as experience/skill (apparent courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience and skill in particular matters (e.g., regular soldiers' familiarity with warlike things) can produce a show of Courage; Socrates considered Courage to be knowledge in this sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'courage' is often conditional: trained/strong fighters appear best not because they are bravest but because of strength/skill; when danger exceeds their means (inferior numbers/resources) they may be first to flee — showing this type is an inferior form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — animal spirit vs moral courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere Animal Spirit (impetuosity, being goaded by pain or instinct) can produce bold actions but is not true Courage unless combined with moral choice and the proper motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wild beasts or those acting from raw impulse or pain are not truly brave. Animal spirit can co-operate with true courage but without reasoned choice it is only a resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — anger/revenge or lust-driven boldness
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldness that arises from anger, desire for revenge, or lust may make one a good fighter but is not true Courage because such actions are driven by present feeling rather than honour or reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characters resemble bravery but lack the honourable motive and rational direction characteristic of true courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — sanguine/hopeful overconfidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence born of frequent victory or intoxication (the Hopeful/Sanguine) is not true Courage; it is based on settled conviction of superiority and collapses when expectations fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: those who run away when events disappoint. True courage is resistant to such failure because it rests on right motive, not mere expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — ignorance (apparent courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done under ignorance may appear brave and are close to the hopeful type but are inferior because the agent lacks a true opinion of himself; when reality is revealed they flee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: troops who attack thinking they face one enemy but flee when they discover otherwise (Argives and Lacedaemonians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage — relation to fear and sudden danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage more properly has fear (and especially painful objects) as its object; better proof of Courage is being fearless and undisturbed under sudden fear than under anticipated danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: with sudden dangers action depends on fixed habit of mind rather than calculation; brave men withstand painful things because it is honourable even while feeling pain. Courage involves endurance of pain for an honourable end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery — object-matter is bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfected Self-Mastery (temperance/moderation) is the mean state with respect to Pleasures, principally bodily pleasures (especially Touch and Taste) rather than mental pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental pleasures (love of honour or learning) do not define this virtue. The senses most implicated in lack of self-control are touch and taste; pleasures of sight/hearing/smell are less central to the vice/virtue distinction here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery — regulates desires by right reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly self-mastering person desires what he ought, in the right manner, and at the right times — i.e., the appetitive principle is accordant with Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs: not pained at the absence of improper pleasures; does not desire improper objects; if he desires bodily pleasures, does so only in moderation and proportionate to health and means. The appetite is obedient and chastened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery — contrast with absence of self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of self-control (unchastened-ness) is shown by taking pleasure in base, brutish objects of touch/taste, excessive desire, and acting so as to increase those desires; the self-master avoids these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: gluttony (grasping beyond natural limit), pleasures that belong to brutes, impulsive grasping that expels Reason. Habit and habituation can cure excess; self-control is more voluntary and blameworthy when lacking because pleasures are objects of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality — mean with respect to Wealth (giving and receiving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality is the mean state concerning Wealth: the Liberal man gives and receives wealth rightly — chiefly characterized by giving to proper persons, in right proportion, and at right times, from a motive of honour, and with pleasure or without pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving (expenditure) is the primary locus of liberality. The liberal person also receives from proper sources (e.g., his own property) to have something to give, but does not receive from improper sources nor ask unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality — giving must be honourable in motive and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts must be given from a motive of honour and in the right fashion; giving to improper people, from wrong motives, or with pain is not Liberality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: giving to flatterers or to subserve one's pleasures is prodigal not liberal. Proper giving follows the 'right giving' pattern: to proper persons, in proportion, at appropriate times, and with positive or at least non-painful feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality — proportionality to one's means
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality depends on the moral state relative to a person's means — the amount given is judged in proportion to the giver's means (one with less who gives proportionally may be more liberal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: assessment of liberality must consider the agent's wealth; inheritors may be thought more liberal because they have not experienced want, but true measure is proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodigality — excess in giving / improper receiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Prodigality is excess in giving (and forbearing to receive) or giving wrongly: spending beyond what is needful, giving to improper people, and often receiving from improper sources to sustain expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodigality differs from liberality because the giving is not honourable or well-measured; it is often a sign of folly rather than deep moral badness and may be corrigible by habituation or want of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stinginess (Meanness) — defect in giving and/or excess in receiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Stinginess (the defect) consists in being deficient in giving and/or excessive in receiving, often marked by base-gaining (receiving from improper sources) or an unwillingness to receive even rightly; it is more congenial to human nature and has many forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms: sparing/close-fisted niggards (deficient in giving), those who refuse to receive (out of shame/fear), and those who receive from improper sources (usurers, brothel-keepers) — the latter are marked by small, disgraceful gain. Stinginess is harder to cure than prodigality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving well is more characteristic of virtue than receiving well
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing well by others (giving) is more corrective and more characteristic of virtue than merely forbearing to receive; praise is given to the giver rather than the one who merely refrains from receiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for assessment: prioritize the moral quality of actions that positively benefit others (giving) when judging liberality or related virtues.
